title: NASA's PRIMA Telescope Would See a Slice of Space Webb Can't Reach
summary: NASA's James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) made headlines for peering at the universe in near- and mid-infrared light. But there's a whole range of infrared wavelengths it can't see — and that's where a new mission comes in. NASA announced that a telescope concept called PRIMA (Probe far-Infrared Mission for Astrophysics) is moving to Phase B, the preliminary design and technology phase. If all goes well, it will launch no earlier than 2033 for a five-year mission. PRIMA's 5.9-foot (1.8-meter) telescope is built to observe the far-infrared — longer wavelengths than JWST is sensitive to. "We can't actually address these science questions with JWST," said Meredith MacGregor, an associate professor at Johns Hopkins University, "because the spectral lines that are required are only in the far-infrared." Those questions include: How much water drives planet formation? What are the total gas masses and carbon and oxygen levels in the disks where exoplanets form? PRIMA would also study how galaxies grow and how supermassive black holes evolve. Lee Armus, a staff scientist at Caltech and the mission's science operations lead, said he's excited about how PRIMA will help scientists understand "the role of powerful molecular outflows in galaxies over cosmic time, and how they shape star formation and the growth of supermassive black holes in the centers of galaxies." The mission has a project cost cap of $1.2 billion, excluding launch — a fraction of JWST's $10 billion. It's the first in a new class called Probe Explorers, designed to sit between flagship missions and smaller efforts. The program traces back to the Explorers Program, which began with Explorer 1 in 1958 and has since flown more than 100 missions. NASA funded two concepts at $5 million each in 2024 and chose PRIMA over the Advanced X-ray Imaging Satellite. "I'm most excited about the things I don't yet know," said Alberto Bolatto, an astronomer at the University of Maryland. "I am elated to be part of the future of astronomy." If it flies, NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory will manage the mission, with contributions from other NASA centers and international partners.
why_it_matters: Astronomy is limited less by imagination than by which wavelengths we can actually collect, so opening the far-infrared is a bit like giving astronomers a new sense — and the tiered mission strategy that produced PRIMA will shape how much science a fixed NASA budget can buy for decades.

background_read: Infrared light is invisible radiation with wavelengths longer than red light; the James Webb Space Telescope (NASA's largest space telescope, launched in 2021) studies the universe in near- and mid-infrared from a position about a million miles from Earth.

Far-infrared wavelengths are even longer, and much of that light is absorbed by water vapour in our atmosphere, which is one reason astronomers need cold space telescopes to observe it; Europe's Herschel Space Observatory was a rare example of a far-infrared mission and operated until 2013.

Spectroscopy splits light into its component wavelengths: atoms and molecules absorb and emit at specific 'spectral lines', so a line that appears only in the far-infrared is the only way to measure certain molecules, such as water and oxygen, in planet-forming disks.

The Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL — a NASA centre in California managed by Caltech that builds and flies many robotic missions, including the Mars rovers) would manage PRIMA if the mission is approved.

NASA's missions are tiered by size and cost: flagships such as JWST are enormous and rare, while Explorer-class missions are smaller and more frequent. The original Explorer 1, launched in 1958, discovered the Van Allen radiation belts around Earth, and the programme has since flown more than a hundred missions.

perspectives.description: PRIMA promises a wavelength range that JWST simply cannot reach, for roughly a tenth of JWST's price. That combination — new science, comparatively modest cost — is exactly what the Probe Explorers class was designed to deliver, and it gives a new generation of researchers access to frontier data.

perspectives.perspective: Critical — budget watchdogs and rival concepts
perspectives.description: A mission that will not launch until the 2030s must survive many years of shifting budgets and political priorities, and its cost cap could still be raised by technical problems. Supporters of the X-ray concept NASA passed over, and of smaller faster missions, argue that money spent on one big probe could fund several quicker experiments.

This is the standard rhythm of space science: big flagships prove a technology, then medium probes make it routine. Far-infrared astronomy has a difficult history — a Japanese-led far-infrared mission, SPICA, was proposed and later cancelled — which shows that the hardest part of these observatories is often funding and cooling technology rather than the science case.

If PRIMA flies, it could survey large numbers of planet-forming disks and galaxy populations rather than studying a handful in detail, turning far-infrared measurements into statistics. The Phase B work on detectors and cooling systems may also feed into whatever far-infrared observatory comes after it.
